Juvenile Brazilian silversides (Atherinella brasiliensis) recruiting into coastal lagoons typically display a total length at puberty of approximately 7.6 centimeters [Lp = approximately 7.6 centimeters], a size threshold that marks the onset of gonadal development and the transition to reproductive competence. Field surveys conducted in the Ubatuba region indicate that individuals attaining this length are capable of participating in the upcoming spawning season. The initial body mass of newly hatched prolarvae derived from the typical egg diameter of 1.6 millimeters observed in the related congener Leuresthes tenuis yields a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0021 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0021 grams], reflecting the modest endogenous yolk reserves that sustain the endotrophic larva during the first few days of development. This reduced birth mass is consistent among atherinopsids with pelagic eggs, where the chorionated embryo relies entirely on stored yolk for energy prior to the onset of exogenous feeding. The substantial fecundity exhibited by females is reflected in an average clutch size of approximately 100 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 100 eggs per spawning event], with multiple clutches produced over an extended breeding season.

At a stable water temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C], the embryonic development of Atherinella brasiliensis proceeds rapidly, with hatching occurring after approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days]. This incubation period is relatively short compared to that of some temperate atherinopsids, reflecting the elevated thermal regime typical of subtropical coastal environments. During the yolk-sac larval stage, the lecithotrophic larva continues to absorb yolk nutrients while the mouth opens and the digestive tract differentiates. The completion of yolk absorption marks the critical trophic switch to exogenous feeding, at which point the actively growing larva must successfully capture planktonic prey to avoid starvation. The timing of this developmental window is tightly coupled to temperature, with warmer conditions accelerating metabolic rates and thus hastening the depletion of yolk reserves. The reproductive frequency under these favorable thermal conditions reaches approximately 30 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 30 spawning events per year], enabling a single female to deposit thousands of eggs over the course of a reproductive season.

Adult females of Atherinella brasiliensis achieve a maximum or ultimate wet weight of approximately 38.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 38.6 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships calibrated against large gravid individuals collected during the peak of the reproductive season. This ultimate body mass is attained after several years of growth, with individuals approaching an asymptotic size that reflects the energetic constraints of a plankton-feeding pelagic fish inhabiting warm coastal waters. Under the same thermal regime of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C], the combination of a clutch size of approximately 100 eggs per spawning event and a frequency of approximately 30 spawning events per year yields an annual reproductive output of approximately 3000 eggs per year. This daily output translates into a substantial annual fecundity, with females producing multiple clutches over an extended spawning period that coincides with the austral summer.

The wet weight at puberty for Brazilian silversides is estimated at approximately 2.8 grams [Wwp = approximately 2.8 grams], a value that aligns with the weight calculated from the species-specific length-weight conversion applied to the total length at puberty. Individuals that have attained this body mass are considered reproductively viable, as they have completed the juvenile phase and entered the adult size range capable of supporting gametogenesis and spawning. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of the species’ nursery habitats, which remain near 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C] for much of the year, the lifespan of Atherinella brasiliensis is estimated at approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years]. This longevity is relatively modest for a fish of its size and indicates a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction over extended somatic persistence. Comparative studies with other atherinopsids of similar body size from tropical and subtropical regions further support the observation that Brazilian silversides complete their life cycle within a relatively compressed temporal window, maximizing reproductive output during the favorable warm season.

The ultimate total length attained by adult Brazilian silversides is approximately 17.7 centimeters [Li = approximately 17.7 centimeters], representing the maximum recorded size for the species based on extensive sampling of coastal lagoon populations along the southeastern Brazilian coast. This maximum length is reached after several years of sustained growth, during which individuals transition from a planktonic larval existence to a benthopelagic feeding habit specialized on zooplankton and small crustaceans. The length-weight relationship derived for this species indicates that the asymptotic body mass of approximately 38.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 38.6 grams] is attained when individuals reach this maximum total length, a pattern consistent with the positive allometric scaling observed in many planktivorous teleosts. The extended spawning season, combined with the moderate fecundity per event, allows a single female to deposit several thousand eggs over the course of a reproductive period, thereby maximizing the probability of larval recruitment despite high rates of early-life mortality typical of pelagic spawners.
